claims.text: Chemical disorder in HEAs induces nanoscale lattice distortions.
Nanoscale lattice distortions from chemical disorder enhance dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning produces dynamic strain aging under cyclic loading.
Dynamic strain aging in HEAs manifests as increased internal friction.
Dynamic strain aging in HEAs shifts the storage modulus relative to conventional alloys.
The HEA will exhibit a more pronounced internal-friction peak than a conventional alloy with low chemical disorder.
The HEA will exhibit a shifted storage-modulus transition relative to a conventional alloy with low chemical disorder.
The magnitudes of the internal-friction and storage-modulus effects correlate with the extent of lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase HEAs containing at least five principal elements in near-equal proportions.
The proposed mechanism applies under cyclic loading across typical engineering temperatures and frequencies.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to multiphase alloys.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to alloys containing significant processing-induced secondary phases.
Prior evidence supports a role for lattice distortions in affecting mechanical properties.
The quantitative relationship between lattice-distortion magnitude and dynamic mechanical response in HEAs remains unclear.
The proposed test uses cyclic dynamic mechanical analysis at frequencies of approximately 1–100 Hz.
The controlled comparison is against a conventional single-phase alloy with similar yield strength and minimal chemical disorder.
Lattice distortion will be quantified using diffraction techniques during the comparison.
A lack of statistically significant internal-friction increase, measurable storage-modulus shift, or correlation with lattice distortion would falsify the hypothesis.
